_meta.descricao: The stages of the Catholic canonization process, from Servant of God to Saint, and related concepts.
_meta.aviso: Simplified explanation of the procedure; specific cases follow particular norms issued by the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints.
fontes_gerais: John Paul II, Apostolic Constitution «Divinus Perfectionis Magister» (1983)

itens.resumo: The public and spontaneous reputation among the faithful that a deceased person lived the Christian virtues heroically or died a martyr — a prerequisite for every cause.
itens.corpo:
The "reputation for holiness" (fama sanctitatis) or "reputation for martyrdom" (fama martyrii) is the informal starting point of any cause of canonization: the spontaneous and widespread perception, among the faithful who knew the person or their story, that he or she lived faith, hope and charity in an extraordinary way — or died as a martyr out of hatred for the faith. The Instruction "Sanctorum Mater" (2007), of the Congregation for the Causes of Saints, is explicit in its article 4: the cause "concerns a Catholic who in life, in death and after death enjoyed a reputation for holiness, living all the Christian virtues in a heroic manner; or enjoys a reputation for martyrdom because, having followed the Lord Jesus Christ more closely, he sacrificed his life in the act of martyrdom". Without this genuine reputation, according to article 7, § 1, the bishop cannot decide to begin the cause: it is necessary to verify that, "among a significant part of the People of God", the Servant of God effectively enjoys this authentic and widespread reputation. The same instruction, in article 25, § 3, in dealing with the presentation of the petition (libellus), determines that the bishop, before accepting it, must verify whether in that period "an authentic reputation for holiness or martyrdom" developed among the People of God.

The qualities this reputation must have in order to be taken seriously were systematized not by a code, but by the classic work of Cardinal Prospero Lambertini, the future Pope Benedict XIV (1740–1758), "De Servorum Dei beatificatione et Beatorum canonizatione", written before his pontificate. It is from there that comes the requirement that the reputation be spontaneous, and not artificially manufactured or promoted by group interests; born among honest and thoughtful people, and not merely occasional enthusiasts; continuous over time, without interruptions or forgetting; growing, and not diminishing as the years pass; and actually present today, not merely the memory of a distant past. The same work of Benedict XIV is cited in the note of "Sanctorum Mater" to define the reputation for holiness as "existimatio seu communis opinio de puritate et integritate vitae, et de virtutibus..., necnon de miraculis eorum intercessione a Deo patratis" — the common opinion about the purity and integrity of life, the virtues and the miracles obtained through their intercession. The same Benedict XIV, in dealing with the revelations and visions of saints and mystics, showed himself discerning: he warned that not every vision reported by a virtuous person is supernatural in character, a criterion of sobriety that runs through his whole approach to holiness.

One should not confuse the reputation for holiness, tied to the life and death of the candidate, with a similar but distinct concept — the "reputation for signs" (fama signorum), treated in its own entry in this collection — which article 6 of "Sanctorum Mater" defines as "the opinion spread among the faithful about the graces and favors received from God through the intercession of the Servant of God". The two reputations reinforce each other: the more solid and persistent the reputation for holiness during life, the greater the readiness of the faithful to seek the candidate's intercession after death, which in turn nourishes the reputation for signs that will later sustain the recognition of a miracle. In the case of martyrdom, the instruction adds that the reputation refers to a death suffered "for the faith or for a virtue connected with the faith".

In practice, it is this reputation that determines the very moment to open the cause, since common law requires waiting five years after death precisely so that the reputation may mature and be distinguished from a passing emotion; when the reputation is considered exceptionally solid, the Pope may dispense with the waiting period — as was done with Mother Teresa of Calcutta (dispensation communicated in early 1999, less than two years after her death) and with John Paul II (dispensation announced by Benedict XVI on May 13, 2005, forty-two days after his death). A fragile, merely local or manipulated reputation, on the other hand, may lead the bishop not to accept the petition and not to institute the diocesan inquiry. The verification of the reputation is therefore not a devotional detail, but the first juridical and pastoral filter of the entire process.

itens.titulo: Opening of the Cause: "Servant of God"
itens.resumo: The initial diocesan phase, in which the local bishop formally authorizes the investigation into the person's life, after verifying the reputation for holiness and obtaining the "nihil obstat" from the Holy See.
itens.corpo:
The cause for canonization formally begins when the bishop of the diocese where the candidate died (or, in specific cases, where he or she lived most significantly) receives from a postulator — see the corresponding entry — the request to open the investigation, the so-called "libellus" (petition), normally accompanied by a biographical memorial and testimony that there is, in fact, a reputation for holiness or martyrdom among the people. The role of the postulator is expressly regulated by the instruction «Sanctorum Mater» (2007, Arts. 12-14): appointed by the "actor" of the cause by means of a mandate, he follows the progress of the inquiry with the diocesan authorities and then in Rome, where, in the Roman phase, he drafts the «positio» — a report that demonstrates the martyrdom or the heroic virtues of the candidate.

Since the «Sanctorum Mater» of 2007, the bishop no longer decides alone. As early as 1969, Paul VI's Constitution «Sacra Rituum Congregatio» had separated the causes of saints from the Congregation of Rites; and it was Saint John Paul II's Constitution «Divinus Perfectionis Magister» (January 25, 1983) that reorganized the entire procedure, together with the «Normae servandae in inquisitionibus ab episcopis faciendis in causis sanctorum» (February 7, 1983). Within this framework, before accepting the petition, the bishop must consult the Congregation for the Causes of Saints and obtain from it the «nihil obstat» — the confirmation that the Holy See sees nothing that would obstruct the cause. Article 45 § 2 of the instruction asks the bishop to send the request accompanied by a brief report with the biographical data of the Servant of God (date, place and diocese of birth and death, activity carried out in the Church, etc.) and the ecclesial importance of the cause.

The common norm requires that five full years be awaited after the candidate's death before this step, a time considered necessary for the reputation for holiness to mature and to be distinguished from a passing emotional reaction tied to the moment of death. The Pope himself, however, may dispense from this period in extraordinary cases. Mother Teresa of Calcutta, who died on September 5, 1997, was granted the dispensation on the occasion of a letter from the Congregation in December 1998, allowing the cause to be opened as early as 1999, less than two years after her death. Even faster was the cause of John Paul II himself: Benedict XVI announced on May 13, 2005, just 42 days after his death, the immediate start of the process, dispensing with the five years "because of the imposing reputation for holiness enjoyed by John Paul II during his life, in his death and after his death." Conversely, the same law provides that the cause not be promoted after about thirty years have passed since death, so as not to lose witnesses and evidence.

From the formal opening of the cause, the person receives the title of "Servant of God," and the diocesan tribunal established for the case begins to gather the testimonies of witnesses who knew him or her — relatives, friends, colleagues at work or in religion, according to a questionnaire (the «interrogatorium») prepared specifically for the case —, in addition to collecting his or her published and unpublished writings, letters, diaries and other relevant documents. Writings already published must first undergo examination by theological censors, who verify that they contain nothing contrary to faith and good morals; only then does the examination of the unpublished writings and of all the biographical documentation gathered proceed. Once this phase is concluded, the acts are sealed and sent to Rome, beginning the Roman phase of the process, described in its own entry in this collection.

itens.titulo: Recognition of Heroic Virtues or Martyrdom
itens.resumo: The Pope declares, by decree, that the person lived the Christian virtues to a heroic degree or suffered martyrdom for the faith, conferring on him or her the title of Venerable.
itens.corpo:
After the documentation gathered by the diocese has been examined, in the Roman phase of the process, by theological consultors and by the Plenary Congregation of Cardinals and Bishops of the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints, the Pope may formally recognize, by decree, that the Servant of God lived the theological virtues—faith, hope, and charity—and the cardinal virtues—prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance—to a heroic degree; or, alternatively, that he or she suffered true martyrdom out of hatred for the faith. The internal path is precise: the Congregation's theologians study the "positio" and, if the vote is favorable by a qualified majority, the dossier passes to the judgment of the bishops and cardinals of the Dicastery; if that judgment is also favorable, the Holy Father authorizes the promulgation of the decree.

The notion of "heroicity" of virtue was established by Benedict XIV in the work "De Servorum Dei beatificatione et Beatorum canonizatione", whose chapters on heroic virtue became classics. According to this formulation, in order to be heroic, a Christian virtue must enable its possessor to perform virtuous actions "with unusual promptness, ease, and pleasure, from supernatural motives and without human reasoning, with self-denial and full control over his natural inclinations." This does not mean the absence of faults or a life without contradictions—many venerables had pasts marked by sin, doubt, or late conversions—but the finding, proven by testimonies and documents, that the person responded constantly and extraordinarily to the grace of God, at a level that clearly surpasses the average behavior even of practicing and sincere faithful. It is this extraordinary quality, and not absolute perfection, that the Church seeks to establish at this stage.

This recognition confers on the person the title of "Venerable", used only in this intermediate period of the process: the Venerable is already proposed by the Church as an example worthy of imitation, but cannot yet receive public liturgical veneration, which is reserved only from beatification onward—according to canon 1187 of the 1983 Code, it is lawful to venerate with public cult only those servants of God who have been inscribed by the authority of the Church in the list of the Saints or the Blessed. Among the venerables recognized in recent decades are the Brazilian Sister Dulce of the Poor—declared venerable before being beatified on May 22, 2011, in Salvador and canonized on October 13, 2019, by Francis, becoming the first saint born in Brazil—and the young man from Rio de Janeiro Guido Schäffer, a physician and surfer.

In the case of martyrdom, the Church dispenses with the requirement of proving heroic virtues throughout the whole of life: the very act of giving one's life out of hatred for the faith is considered sufficient and culminating proof of love for Christ, and since the first centuries the martyr has been held to have immediate entry into glory. For this reason, for martyrs a miracle is not required as a condition even for beatification: "Greater love has no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends" (John 15:13). This direct path to beatification is treated in more detail in the entry on martyrdom in this same collection. Finally, it should be noted that from 2017 the motu proprio "Maiorem hac dilectionem" of Francis added to heroic virtue and martyrdom a third path: the "offering of life", for those who voluntarily give themselves up to certain and premature death out of charity.

itens.resumo: The confirmation of a miracle (waived for martyrs) allows beatification, a pontifical act of public worship still restricted to a diocese, region or religious family — and which, unlike canonization, is not held to be infallible.
itens.corpo:
Beatification is the intermediate stage between the declaration of Venerable and canonization. For those who died as "confessors" — that is, without shedding their blood for the faith — the confirmation of a miracle obtained through their intercession after death is as a rule required, almost always a complete, instantaneous, lasting and scientifically inexplicable physical healing, attributed to prayers addressed specifically to the candidate. The Church does not require a miracle for martyrs, whose very witness of blood is already considered sufficient proof of radical union with Christ; the Pope may grant them beatification solely on the basis of the official recognition of martyrdom (see the separate entry on martyrdom).

The alleged miracle is first subjected to rigorous examination by the Vatican Medical Board (see the separate entry), made up of experts "both believers and non-believers", and only after the impossibility of a scientific explanation has been confirmed does it proceed to theological evaluation, which verifies whether the healing in fact occurred in connection with the invocation of the Venerable. Once the miracle has been approved by the theological consultors, by the cardinals and bishops gathered in Plenary Congregation and, finally, by the Pope himself — who authorizes the decree —, the date of the beatification ceremony is set.

Until 2005 the pontiff himself used to preside over the rites of beatification; in that year Benedict XVI decided to resume the long-standing practice of delegating the celebration to a representative of his, as a rule the Prefect of the Congregation for the Causes of Saints. According to the Congregation's communiqué of September 29, 2005, signed by Prefect José Saraiva Martins and Secretary Edward Nowak, beatification "is always a pontifical act", but it will be celebrated by a representative of the Holy Father; canonization, which "grants the Blessed the cult for the whole Church", remains reserved to the Pope himself. The same communiqué establishes that the rite is to take place in the diocese that promoted the cause (or in another suitable place), and may take place in Rome at the request of the bishops and postulators, and that it is to be held during Mass, "unless particular liturgical reasons suggest" the celebration of the Liturgy of the Word or the Liturgy of the Hours. The Congregation's explanatory document, also of September 29, 2005, justifies the decision by two requirements: "to highlight to a greater extent in the manner of celebration the substantial difference between beatification and canonization" and "to involve the particular Churches in a more visible way". Thus, the first beatification of the new pontificate, on May 14, 2005 (the Servants of God Ascensión Nicol Goñi and Marianne Cope), was presided over by Cardinal José Saraiva Martins "de mandato Summi Pontificis"; on June 19, 2005, in Warsaw, the rite was presided over by Cardinal Józef Glemp, Primate of Poland.

Beatification authorizes public worship of the new Blessed, but in a restricted form: to the diocese of origin, a specific region, a country or the religious family to which he or she belonged, and not yet to the whole universal Church — a fundamental distinction that separates it from canonization (see the separate entry in this collection). It is from beatification, and not before, that churches may display images of the Blessed for public veneration, dedicate altars to him or her, and include his or her memorial in the local liturgical calendar. It is the common opinion of theologians that the Pope is infallible when pronouncing a canonization (the decree is an irreformable decision), but this infallibility does not extend to beatification, which is always "permission, not command" — a worship that is permitted, not prescribed for the whole Church.

The entire procedure today rests on the Apostolic Constitution Divinus perfectionis Magister, of John Paul II (January 25, 1983), which profoundly reformed the causes of saints and provided the Congregation with a College of Relators, and on the complementary norms of February 7, 1983, in addition to the Instruction Sanctorum Mater (May 17, 2007), approved by Benedict XVI. The 1983 Code of Canon Law, in canon 1403 § 1, expressly refers these causes to "special pontifical law" — that is, common law does not directly regulate them. To these sources was added the Apostolic Letter "Maiorem hac dilectionem" of Francis (motu proprio of July 11, 2017), which introduced a fourth path to beatification, the "offering of life": for one who, moved by charity, freely and voluntarily accepted certain and premature death for the sake of neighbor, without it being properly martyrdom (there is no persecutor) or heroic virtues (there is no prolonged exercise).

There is also a frequent but little-mentioned material dimension. The causes involve costs of research, translation, historical and medical expertise, and ceremonies: an average cost of around 500,000 euros per beatification is reported (allegedly possibly exceeding 1 million in causes of great visibility), and the opacity of these expenses has given rise to criticism of rising costs and "price menus". In response, Francis published in March 2016 new norms for the administration of the goods of the causes — giving diocesan bishops and religious superiors the power to approve and oversee budgets —, and the Dicastery released a table of expected fees. Among the causes concluded up to 2020, there are about 3,003 beatifications and 1,479 canonizations since the creation of the Congregation (1969), according to data released by the Dicastery itself.

itens.resumo: The confirmation of a second miracle (subsequent to beatification) leads to canonization, an act reserved to the Pope, which extends the veneration of the saint to the entire universal Church; it belongs to the "practical infallibility" of the magisterium.
itens.corpo:
Except for martyrs, canonization requires the confirmation of a second miracle, occurring after the beatification ceremony and attributed to the intercession of the one already Blessed — investigated with the same scientific and theological rigor as the first, beginning with the Medical Board, passing through the theological consultors and the Plenary Congregation before reaching the Pope's final decision. In the case of martyrs, a miracle subsequent to beatification is also ordinarily required, but, depending on the nature of the martyrdom, the Pope may dispense with it. Unlike beatification, which since 2005 has usually been presided over by a cardinal representing the pontiff, canonization remains an act reserved exclusively to the Pope, celebrated personally by him, traditionally in Saint Peter's Square — as in the great ceremonies of April 27, 2014, when Francis simultaneously canonized John XXIII and John Paul II.

With canonization, the Church declares that the person is definitively in the glory of God and inscribes his or her name in the catalogue — the "canon" — of the saints, authorizing and recommending public veneration throughout the Catholic Church, with the right to a proper liturgical memorial in the universal calendar or, at least, in the particular calendars of countries, dioceses or religious institutes. Unlike the Blessed, whose veneration is restricted, the Saint may be publicly invoked, have churches dedicated to his or her name, and have images venerated anywhere in the Catholic world. It should be noted that, unlike canonization, beatification is neither a definitive nor an infallible act: after it, the cause is submitted to a new complete examination with a view to canonization, which would make no sense if beatification were definitive in character.

The reform of the procedure is due to the Apostolic Constitution Divinus perfectionis Magister of John Paul II (January 25, 1983), which replaced the system in force since the reorganization carried out by Paul VI in 1969. The task of regulating divine worship and handling the causes of saints went back to the Sacred Congregation of Rites, created by Sixtus V by the Constitution "Immensa Aeterni Dei" of January 22, 1588; on May 8, 1969, with "Sacra Rituum Congregatio," Paul VI divided it into two dicasteries, one for Divine Worship and another for the Causes of Saints. Under Divinus perfectionis Magister, causes came to be investigated by the diocesan bishops themselves and supervised by a College of Relators. The dicastery changed its name over time: Congregation for the Causes of Saints (1988, by Pastor Bonus) and, in 2022, with Francis's Praedicate Evangelium, Dicastery for the Causes of Saints. Between 1594 and 2014, the Catholic Church proclaimed about 1,600 saints.

As to the value of the act, the Doctrinal Commentary on the Concluding Formula of the Profession of Faith, published by the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith on June 29, 1998, and signed by the then Prefect, Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, expressly cites "the canonizations of saints" among the truths "connected with revelation by historical necessity," which must be held definitively (the so-called "dogmatic facts"). The question, however, has never been the object of a solemn ex cathedra definition. Saint Thomas Aquinas, in the only mention he makes of the subject, wrote that canonization lies between the truths of faith and judgments on particular facts, since "the honor we render to the saints is a certain profession of faith," concluding that "we must piously believe that in this matter too the judgment of the Church cannot be false" (Quodlibet IX, 16). Benedict XIV, in the eighteenth century, taught, in his "De canonizatione sanctorum" (Book I, ch. 43), that the infallibility of the act of canonization had not yet been defined as a truth of faith, but that to deny it would amount at least to rashness — "rash, scandalous and savoring of heresy." The position most widely accepted among theologians today is that canonization belongs to the "practical infallibility" of the magisterium (which also encompasses general laws, the approval of religious orders and liturgical rites), it being theologically difficult to conceive that the Church would proclaim as a universal intercessor someone who was not already in the presence of God.

itens.titulo: The Medical and Theological Examination of Miracles
itens.resumo: Cases of allegedly miraculous healing go through a medical commission of experts — believers and non-believers alike — and then through theologians, before any official recognition.
itens.corpo:
Cases of physical healing presented as a miracle first go through a medical commission of the Holy See — the Medical Board (Consulta Medica) —, made up of specialists «both believers and non-believers», who verify whether the healing is complete, lasting, and scientifically inexplicable by current medical knowledge. The participation of physicians in canonization processes is ancient: already in the medieval period experts were consulted, and Benedict XIV, on September 17, 1743, created a specific Register (Albo) of medical experts. Pius XII, on October 20, 1948, established a Commission of Physicians within the then Congregation of Sacred Rites and, on December 15 of the same year, a special Medical Council. John XXIII, on July 10, 1959, merged these two bodies into a single Medical Board, approving its Regulations.

Its internal functioning is governed by its own regulations. The previous version was approved by Paul VI on April 23, 1976, in light of the Constitution «Sacra Rituum Congregatio» of 1969; the work of revision began in September 2015, and the current text was approved by Pope Francis on August 24, 2016 and published on September 23, 2016. Under these regulations, the Medical Board that examines each case is composed of seven members — including the President and the two ex officio Experts —, and is valid only if at least six of the seven take part. The experts are chosen by the Secretary of the Congregation, on the proposal of the Undersecretary, and summoned about one month in advance; if necessary, experts «ad casum» from outside the Register may be called upon. When the alleged case is not a healing — for example, remaining unharmed in a danger, or multiplications —, technical experts are appointed, and the Technical Board proceeds in a manner analogous to the Medical Board.

The decision to move forward requires a qualified majority of at least 5/7 or 4/6, and a case examined three times with a suspensive or negative result may not be presented again; in the event of a re-examination, new experts must be summoned, and a re-examination is presided over by a physician of the Register appointed by the Prefect. If the two ex officio expert votes are both negative, the Undersecretary communicates this to the Postulator, who may request the vote of a third ex officio expert; if that vote is also negative, one may not proceed ad ulteriora. The regulations impose secrecy on everyone involved — promoters of the cause, tribunal, postulators, experts, and officials of the dicastery, especially when the person healed is a minor — and require that the honorarium for the experts be paid by bank transfer, in the name of transparency; the office of President of the Medical Board allows only one reconfirmation (five years plus five). The documents sent to each expert include the «Fattispecie Cronologica», the «Summarium» and the medico-legal reports of the ex officio experts. The Secretary, the Undersecretary and the Promoter of the Faith attend the session without voting rights; at the request of the Postulation, experts for the party may also be admitted, who do not take part in the vote. It is ultimately for the Pope to «recognize an extraordinary event as a true miracle».

Only after the medical stage is the case examined theologically, to verify whether the healing in fact occurred in connection with the invocation of the candidate for sainthood; with regard to miracles, the Undersecretary performs the functions that «Divinus perfectionis Magister» assigns to the relator. The opening of the diocesan phase that gathers this evidence is governed by the Instruction «Sanctorum Mater» (May 17, 2007) and by the Apostolic Constitution «Divinus perfectionis Magister» (January 25, 1983), which requires that investigations be conducted «diligently seeking the historical truth». The theological evaluation is followed by the opinion of the cardinals and bishops and by the Pope's authorization for the decree. The Vatican's own newspaper sums up the purpose of the norms: «the good of the causes, which can never dispense with the historical and scientific truth of the alleged miracles».

itens.titulo: Martyrdom as a Direct Path to Beatification
itens.resumo: When martyrdom "in hatred of the faith" is recognized, the Church waives the requirement of a miracle for beatification.
itens.corpo:
In the ordinary procedure, the beatification of a Servant of God requires the verification of a miracle attributed to his or her intercession — usually a healing considered scientifically inexplicable by a medical commission. When, however, the Church recognizes that the person was killed specifically "in hatred of the faith" (in odium fidei), and not for merely political, personal or random reasons, this requirement is waived: the very witness of martyrdom is already considered sufficient proof of radical union with Christ. The candidate declared a martyr immediately becomes Blessed, without the need for a prior miracle.

The reason is above all theological and goes back to the ancient tradition of the Church, taken up again by the Second Vatican Council: the Dogmatic Constitution «Lumen Gentium» (no. 50) calls martyrdom the "supreme witness of faith and charity", the highest level of holiness, as at the origin of the Church. If blood shed for Christ is the supreme proof, no additional sign is asked for. A miracle is still required, however, for the subsequent canonization: a Blessed who is a martyr still needs a second miracle, occurring after the beatification, for inscription in the catalogue of the saints venerated by the whole Church.

The distinction between beatification and canonization was consolidated historically. Canonizations became the exclusive prerogative of the Pontiff by decision of Gregory IX in 1234; over the course of the sixteenth century, a distinction came to be made between beatification (recognition of holiness with local cult) and canonization (universal cult). From the seventeenth century on, with the decrees of Urban VIII, and above all with the Apostolic Constitution «Divinus Perfectionis Magister» of John Paul II (January 25, 1983), the procedure was deeply reformed, with the aim of achieving simplicity, speed and effectiveness. It is in the legislation after 1983 that the practice of beatifying martyrs without the prior approval of a miracle is established.

Concrete cases illustrate this path. The Martyrs of Cunhaú and Uruaçu, in Rio Grande do Norte — Father André de Soveral, Father Ambrósio Francisco Ferro, the layman Mateus Moreira and 27 other companions, killed in 1645 during the Dutch occupation for refusing to abandon the Catholic faith and adopt Calvinism — were beatified in Rome on March 5, 2000, and canonized on October 15, 2017, by Pope Francis, becoming the first martyr saints of Brazil. On that occasion, the Archbishop of Natal, Dom Jaime Vieira Rocha, explained that, "in the case of old processes involving martyrdom", miracles are dispensed with, a prerogative of the Pope.

This case must be distinguished from so-called equipollent (or equivalent) canonization, a distinct instrument used when the Pope, after verification, approves a cult that is already ancient and well established without requiring a proven miracle — it requires the antiquity and constancy of the cult, historical attestation of Catholic faith, and a reputation for holiness. It was by equipollence that Francis canonized, among others, Angela of Foligno (2013), Peter Faber (2013) and Saint José de Anchieta (2014). In addition, on July 11, 2017, with the Apostolic Letter issued motu proprio «Maiorem hac dilectionem», Francis created a third path to beatification, the "offering of life" (oblatio vitae): a Christian who freely offers his or her life and accepts a certain and premature death out of charity — but whose case fits neither martyrdom nor heroic virtue — may be beatified, provided that a miracle after his or her death is proven.

itens.resumo: A title that associates an already canonized saint with the special protection of a place, profession, cause or group of people — a devotion distinct from the old "right of patronage."
itens.corpo:
"Patronage" or the "patron saint" is a devotional practice, not a formal stage of the canonization process: it associates an already canonized saint with special intercession for a country, city, diocese, profession, illness or specific cause. The choice usually stems from a biographical connection with the saint (Saint Joseph, a carpenter, is the patron of workers) or from a consolidated historical and devotional bond. Patronage presupposes that the saint has already been inscribed by the authority of the Church in the catalogue of the Saints or Blessed, and the designation is normally made by the Holy See at the request of episcopal conferences or local communities.

The Code of Canon Law (1983), in treating the veneration of the saints (Title IV, canons 1186-1190), establishes in canon 1187 that "it is permitted to venerate with public cult only those servants of God who have been listed in the catalogue of the saints or the blessed by the authority of the Church." Canon 1186 recommends to the filial veneration of the faithful the Blessed Virgin Mary and promotes the cult of the other saints, "by whose example the faithful are edified and by whose intercession they are sustained." It is within this framework of worship that the figure of the patron saint is situated.

One should not confuse devotional patronage with the old "right of patronage" (ius patronatus), a legal institution of medieval origin that granted laypeople or sovereigns the right to present candidates for ecclesiastical benefices in churches they had founded or endowed. Classical canon law summed up its requirements in the formula patronum faciunt dos, aedificatio, fundus — the endowment, the building and the land. This right of patronage — which in colonial Brazil came to be exercised by the kings of Portugal as the Royal Patronage (Padroado Real) — is a historical reality distinct from the simple devotion to a patron saint.

The Brazilian case is illustrative. After the Marian Congress held in September 1929, through the efforts of the then Archbishop of Rio de Janeiro, Dom Sebastião Leme, and of the rector of the Shrine of Aparecida, the Redemptorist Father Antão Jorge Hechenblaickner — an Austrian from Ampass, born on June 5, 1880, ordained in 1904 and rector of the shrine from 1927 — Pope Pius XI accepted the bishops' request and, on July 16, 1930, signed the decree proclaiming Our Lady of the Conception Aparecida Principal Patroness of Brazil. The official proclamation was celebrated in Rio de Janeiro, then the federal capital, on May 31, 1931, gathering about a million people, with an open-air Mass in front of the Church of São Francisco de Paula, followed by a procession to the Esplanada do Castelo, in the presence of President Getúlio Vargas and the apostolic nuncio Dom Aloísio Masella. It was the first time the original image of Aparecida left its shrine, transported by train to the capital.

The devotion had been recognized earlier by other popes: Leo XIII granted in 1895 permission to celebrate its feast on the first Sunday of May; Pius X signed the decree of coronation in 1904 and that of the dignity of Minor Basilica in 1908. Later, Pius XII elevated Aparecida to an archdiocese in 1958 and Paul VI offered the Golden Rose in 1967; Benedict XVI did the same in 2007. Federal Law No. 6,802, of June 30, 1980 — a bill by Deputy Jorge Arbage — declared October 12 a national holiday "for public and official worship of Our Lady Aparecida, Patroness of Brazil," definitively linking the ecclesiastical title to civil legislation.

itens.resumo: Official representative who conducts a cause for beatification or canonization before the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints.
itens.corpo:
The postulator is the person — priest, religious brother or sister, or layperson — charged with conducting a cause for canonization from a juridical standpoint, from the diocesan phase until the final decision of the Holy See. He or she represents the petitioner of the cause (the one who promotes it) and the community of the faithful before the competent authority, first the diocesan bishop and then the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints (formerly the Congregation, renamed in 2022 by the Constitution «Praedicate Evangelium»). It is the postulator's task to gather the documentation, collect the testimony of witnesses, organize the proofs of the reputation for holiness and, when one is alleged, oversee the investigation of possible miracles attributed to the candidate.

The office requires specific training in theology, canon law and history, as well as knowledge of the practices of the Dicastery. It is advisable to appoint, from the beginning, a postulator residing in Rome and a vice-postulator in the diocese; the appointments must be approved by the diocesan bishop and, in the Roman phase, confirmed by the Dicastery. The large religious orders — Franciscans, Dominicans and Jesuits, among others — usually designate postulators general from among their members, who develop a reputation as experts and have their offices in Rome.

The document that governs the function is the «Regulations for Postulators» of the Dicastery, which brings together the practice and the pontifical law on the causes of saints, contained in the Code of Canon Law, the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches, the Constitution «Divinus Perfectionis Magister», the «Normae servandae in Inquisitionibus ab Episcopis faciendis in Causis Sanctorum», the Apostolic Letter «Maiorem hac dilectionem» and the Instructions «Sanctorum Mater» and «Relics in the Church». Among the requirements, the postulator must hold a diploma from the School of Advanced Formation in the Causes of Saints, present his or her curriculum vitae and academic titles, and take an oath to fulfill the office faithfully and to keep secrecy. The current regulations, approved under the pontificate of Francis, limit each postulator to a maximum number of active causes (about 30) and prohibit holding the office together with certain ecclesiastical offices.

In the diocesan phase, which begins with a libellus (a written petition) addressed to the bishop of the place where the Servant of God died, the postulator gathers the biography, the candidate's authentic writings and the list of witnesses, assisting the bishop in the inquiry. Once this phase is concluded, all the material is sent to Rome. In the Roman phase, the postulator works side by side with the relator (or ponens) appointed by the Dicastery in drawing up the «positio», the document that synthesizes the life, the virtues or the martyrdom, and the reputation for holiness of the candidate — currently the Dicastery asks that the positio not exceed about 500 pages.

The positio is then examined by theological consultors and, in the case of "historical causes" (those of candidates who lived long ago and for whom there are no eyewitnesses), also by a commission of historians. If the votes are favorable by a qualified majority, the dossier is submitted to the judgment of the cardinals and bishops of the Dicastery and, finally, to the Holy Father, who authorizes the promulgation of the Decree on the heroicity of the virtues or on martyrdom. The postulator also administers the funds collected for the cause and is bound to secrecy regarding the acts of the inquiry. Historically, the office took shape with the reforms following 1983; before that, analogous functions were exercised by procurators and advocates before the former Congregation of Rites.

itens.resumo: Volume prepared in the Roman phase of the cause, under the guidance of a relator of the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints, by which the postulator gathers and argues the documentary and testimonial evidence on the life, virtues or martyrdom of a candidate for sainthood.
itens.corpo:
The «positio» is the volume prepared in the Roman phase of the cause, under the guidance of a relator appointed by the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints, by which the postulator demonstrates that the Servant of God lived the Christian virtues to a heroic degree or suffered martyrdom out of hatred for the faith. Its full Latin title indicates its object: «Positio super Vita, Virtutibus et Fama Sanctitatis», in the case of virtues, or «Positio super Martyrio», in the case of martyrdom. Since the motu proprio «Maiorem hac dilectionem» of Pope Francis, dated July 11, 2017, a «Positio» on the «offering of life» (oblatio vitae) has been added to these, which introduced a fourth path to beatification, distinct from martyrdom and from the heroicity of virtues, for those who freely and voluntarily offered their own lives for their neighbor, accepting certain and premature death out of charity.

The volume is organized into main parts: the Biography, reconstructed from the documentation gathered in the diocesan phase; the «Informatio», the postulator's argumentative exposition, which demonstrates the heroicity of the virtues or the reality of the martyrdom and of the reputation for holiness; and the «Summarium Testium», an organized compilation of the witnesses' depositions, accompanied by the candidate's writings and other documents. The distinction between these parts was established by the reform of John Paul II, and the scale of the work is considerable: the «Positio» of Pope John Paul I, delivered on October 17, 2016, consists of 3,650 pages in five volumes, the result of about ten years of research; that of Álvaro del Portillo, presented on February 19, 2010, comprises 2,530 pages in three volumes. The norms of the Dicastery require that the «Positio» generally not exceed 500 pages, except in particular cases.

Once completed and printed, the positio is submitted to the opinion of a group of theologians — the Special Congress of Theological Consultors, which in practice brings together about nine consultors — who vote on the merits of the cause; in the case of a «historical cause» — of a candidate who lived a long time ago, without eyewitnesses — it is also examined by a Historical Consultation, chaired by the Relator General together with the group of history consultors, which verifies the scientific value and the sufficiency of the body of evidence. The submission norms prescribe copies with a gray cover for the historical examination and with a red cover, enclosing the «Relatio et Vota», after the positive result. Once approved by a qualified majority, the dossier passes to the judgment of the bishops and cardinals, members of the Dicastery; one of them, designated by the prefect as ponens, prepares the written vote delivered to the Holy Father. It is then for the Pope to decide on the promulgation of the decree on heroic virtues or on martyrdom, by which the Servant of God comes to be called «Venerable».

The juridical instrument of the positio derives from the Apostolic Constitution «Divinus Perfectionis Magister» of January 25, 1983, and from the «Normae servandae in inquisitionibus ab episcopis faciendis in causis sanctorum» of February 7, 1983, which profoundly reformed the procedure and provided the then Congregation with a College of Relators, charged with overseeing the preparation of the «positiones». Among the relators there is one specially charged with the study of the «Positiones» on miracles, who takes part in the Consultation of Physicians and the Congress of Theologians. A recent example is the positio of the Servant of God Sister Lúcia of Jesus and of the Immaculate Heart, delivered to the Dicastery on October 13, 2022, with Monsignor Maurizio Tagliaferri as relator; studied by the theologians on March 9, 2023, and approved by the cardinals and bishops on June 6, 2023, it led to her being declared Venerable by Francis on June 22, 2023.

itens.resumo: An office created by Sixtus V in 1587 to formally question the evidence in a canonization; it found its greatest theorist in Benedict XIV and was reformed by John Paul II in 1983, when the critical task passed to the Promoter of Justice.
itens.corpo:
The office of Promoter of the Faith (in Latin, «Promotor Fidei») was established by Pope Sixtus V in 1587, in the context of the reorganization of canonization causes undertaken by the post-Tridentine Church. Its function consisted in presenting, in writing, every possible argument — even seemingly minor ones — against raising someone to the honors of the altar: it questioned the soundness of the alleged miracles, pointed out inconsistencies in testimonies, and tested the authenticity of the candidate's reputation for holiness. Acting against him was the «advocatus Dei» (God's Advocate), charged with upholding the petition. From the position taken by the Promoter of the Faith, who seemed to take the opposing side, came the popular nickname «devil's advocate» («advocatus diaboli»).

The office did not come out of nowhere: an analogous figure already appears in the preliminary work for the beatification of Saint Lawrence Justinian (1381-1456), under Pope Leo X (1513-1521) — although the beatification only took place in 1524, under Clement VII. The exact date of the institution varies among the sources: 1587 is the most frequently cited year for the creation of the office by Sixtus V, while the Apostolic Constitution «Immensa Aeterni Dei», of January 22, 1588, established the Sacred Congregation of Rites, to which was entrusted both the regulation of divine worship and the study of the causes of saints. It was within this Congregation that the Promoter of the Faith became established at the end of the sixteenth century; in 1708, it became one of the most important offices of the Congregation.

The most famous holder of the office was Prospero Lorenzo Lambertini (1675-1758). On April 7, 1708, Clement XI separated the office of Promoter of the Faith from that of «promotor fiscalis» and appointed Lambertini coadjutor of the Promoter of the Faith; in 1712 he was promoted to Promoter General of the Faith, a post he held until 1728. From this experience was born his monumental work «De Servorum Dei Beatificatione et Beatorum Canonizatione», written between 1734 and 1738 — before his pontificate — and revised between 1747 and 1751 as Pope. The treatise, sometimes compared to the Summa Theologiae of Saint Thomas with regard to canonization causes, codified rigorous criteria for the discernment of miracles and united theology, law, and the nascent medical science. Elected Pope in 1740 with the name Benedict XIV, he remained linked to the history of the canonization process as its greatest theoretical legislator.

Under the Congregation of Rites, the Promoter of the Faith appeared before the Pope to present the case against canonization; if his objections were refuted and the process came to an end, he was brought again into the presence of the Pontiff to publicly withdraw the case. It was this adversarial structure that the Apostolic Constitution «Divinus Perfectionis Magister», of John Paul II (January 25, 1983), completely reformulated. Under n. 10 of the document, the Congregation for the Causes of Saints came to have a «Promoter of the Faith or Prelate Theologian», whose task is to preside over the Congress of Theologians (where he votes), to prepare the report on that Congress, and to take part, as an expert but without a vote, in the Congregation of the Cardinals and Bishops; the Cardinal Prefect may also appoint a Promoter of the Faith «ad casum» for specific causes. The task of ensuring the juridical integrity of the cause was entrusted to the «Promoter of Justice» («Promotor Iustitiae»).

In practice, the former «devil's advocate» lost the weight it had held for almost four centuries, which, for critics of the reform, made the process potentially less rigorous in examining objections; the office, however, was not simply suppressed, but transformed. The Holy See may still request the testimony of critics in controversial cases: in the beatification process of Mother Teresa of Calcutta, the atheist writer and journalist Christopher Hitchens — author of the documentary and the book «The Missionary Position» (1995) — was invited by Fr. David O'Connor, of the Archdiocese of Washington, to testify as «advocatus diaboli», giving his testimony in 2003 and recounting the episode in an article in Vanity Fair (October 2001) and later in Slate (October 20, 2003). The number of canonizations accelerated after 1983: about 300 canonizations in the period from 1587 to 1983, against approximately 500 canonizations and more than 1,300 beatifications between 1983 and 2005 alone, during the pontificate of John Paul II.

itens.titulo: Dicastery for the Causes of Saints
itens.resumo: Body of the Roman Curia that prepares and examines all causes of beatification and canonization of the Catholic Church, headquartered in the Palazzo delle Congregazioni ai Propilei, in Piazza Pio XII, in Rome.
itens.corpo:
The origin of this body goes back to the Sacred Congregation of Rites, created by Pope Sixtus V with the Apostolic Constitution «Immensa Aeterni Dei» of January 22, 1588, which reorganized the Roman Curia into permanent congregations and entrusted to this dicastery both the discipline of divine worship and the study of the causes of saints. The idea of dividing the Congregation of Rites into two dicasteries had already been raised in the commission for the reform of the Curia convened by Saint Pius X, but it would only be carried out decades later. On August 15, 1967, Paul VI restructured the dicastery by creating two sections, the second, judicial, being the one that regulated the canonization procedure.

On May 8, 1969, Pope Paul VI, by the Apostolic Constitution «Sacra Rituum Congregatio», definitively suppressed the Sacred Congregation of Rites and divided its functions between two new congregations: the Congregation for Divine Worship and the Discipline of the Sacraments and the Congregation for the Causes of Saints. This new congregation then received its own structure, organized into three offices: the judicial office, that of the Promoter General of the Faith, and the historical-hagiographical office, the latter continuing the Historical Section created by Pius XI on February 6, 1930. The new congregation inherited the entire historical archive of the Rites.

On January 25, 1983, John Paul II promulgated the Apostolic Constitution «Divinus Perfectionis Magister» and, on February 7 of the same year, the «Normae servandae», which profoundly reformed the procedure of the causes and restructured the Congregation, providing it with a College of Relators charged with overseeing the preparation of the «positiones» of the Servants of God. On June 28, 1988, the Apostolic Constitution «Pastor Bonus» confirmed its name as the Congregation for the Causes of Saints. On March 19, 2022, Pope Francis published the Apostolic Constitution «Praedicate Evangelium», in force since June 5, 2022, which transformed it into the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints (in Latin, «Dicasterium de Causis Sanctorum»). Articles 98 to 102 of «Praedicate Evangelium» define its competences: to deal, according to the prescribed procedure, with everything concerning the causes of beatification and canonization; to give special norms and assist diocesan bishops in the preparation of causes; to examine the acts of causes already prepared and to give a judgment on their merits, submitting them to the Roman Pontiff; to oversee the administration of the Fund for the property of the causes; to establish the procedure for verifying and declaring the authenticity of relics; and to judge concerning the granting of the title of Doctor of the Church, after the vote of the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith.

The cause goes through an authentic, widespread and lasting «reputation of holiness» and has a first phase in the diocese; once it arrives in Rome, a relator is assigned who guides the postulator in preparing the positio. This is studied by a group of theologians and, in the case of a «historical cause», also by a commission of historians; if the opinion is favorable, the dossier passes to the ordinary session of cardinals and bishops. In view of the Jubilee of 2025, Pope Francis established, within the Dicastery, the «Commission of the New Martyrs — Witnesses to the Faith» (letter of July 5, 2023), to compile a Catalogue of those, including those of other Christian confessions, who shed their blood for Christ, in an «ecumenism of blood», distinguishing it from any new canonical criterion for ascertaining martyrdom.

Its headquarters is the Palazzo delle Congregazioni ai Propilei, also called Palazzo dei Propilei, at Piazza Pio XII, 10, in Rome, a modernist-style building constructed in the first half of the twentieth century and opened on May 25, 1936, designed by the architect Giuseppe Momo, which houses several dicasteries and offices of the Curia. The prefect is Cardinal Marcello Semeraro, appointed by Francis on October 15, 2020, to succeed Cardinal Giovanni Angelo Becciu; the secretary is Archbishop Fabio Fabene and the undersecretary is Father Bogusław Stanisław Turek, C.S.M.A. Among the prefects emeriti are Cardinals José Saraiva Martins, Angelo Amato and Giovanni Angelo Becciu.

itens.resumo: An extraordinary form of canonization, without the ordinary process and without a proven miracle, by which the Pope extends to the universal Church an ancient and uninterrupted cult already rendered to the saint.
itens.corpo:
Equipollent canonization (or "by equivalence") is an exceptional procedure by which the Pope inscribes a saint in the catalogue of the universal Church without requiring the complete ordinary process, including the verification of miracles. The proofs normally gathered in the canonical stages — an ancient and uninterrupted public cult, incontestable historical testimony to the virtues or martyrdom, and a lasting reputation for miraculous intercession — are considered, taken together, as "equivalent" to the entire process. The act is accomplished by a simple pontifical decree, without the solemn ceremony of canonization, and, according to canonists, enjoys the same definitive character as ordinary canonizations. The current normative foundation is canon 1187 of the 1983 Code of Canon Law, which reserves to the authority of the Church the inscription in the album of the saints and blessed; the practice, of more ancient origin, was systematized in the eighteenth century by Benedict XIV in the work «De Servorum Dei Beatificatione et Beatorum Canonizatione».

The doctrine carefully distinguishes equipollent canonization from equipollent beatification. The latter concerns the "ancient blessed" — servants of God who enjoy public cult "ab immemorabili tempore" —, that is, those whose cult developed between the end of the pontificate of Alexander III († 1181) and 1534, according to the Apostolic Constitution «Caelestis Hierusalem Cives» of Urban VIII (1634). When the decree confirming the cult is published without prior demonstration of martyrdom, heroic virtues or offering of life, it is still necessary to conduct an inquiry into the life of the candidate before canonization is considered. The distinction avoids confusing two different juridical acts: the extension to the whole Church of an already existing cult and the formal recognition of virtues or martyrdom through the ordinary process.

The procedure is used sparingly, above all for figures of long-established veneration for centuries, whose ordinary process would be difficult to conduct for lack of eyewitnesses or recent documentation. The modern list includes, among others: Albert the Great, Thomas More and John Fisher (by Pius XI, 1931 and 1935); Margaret of Hungary (Pius XII, 1943); Gregory Barbarigo (John XXIII, 1960); John of Ávila and Nikola Tavelić (Paul VI, 1970); the martyrs of Trnava/Košice (John Paul II, 1995); Saint Hildegard of Bingen, canonized equipollently by Benedict XVI on May 10, 2012, 833 years after her death; and, under Francis, Angela of Foligno (October 9, 2013), Peter Faber (December 17, 2013) and Saint Joseph of Anchieta (April 3, 2014), canonized 416 years after his death. In 2017 the same procedure was applied to the thirty Martyrs of Cunhaú and Uruaçu, protomartyrs of Brazil, beatified by John Paul II in 2000.

Among the cases frequently cited alongside equipollence is that of Saint John XXIII. Canonized on April 27, 2014 in the same ceremony as Saint John Paul II, Roncalli was raised to the altars "pro gratia", that is, without proof of a second miracle. The justification given was not exactly formal equipollence, but the exceptional breadth of the liturgical cult already rendered to the blessed — whose memorial, officially inscribed in the calendars of particular churches in various parts of the world, with prior authorization of the Holy See, was already similar to that of a canonized saint. The case illustrates how the dispensation from the miracle, in its various forms, remains reserved to the discernment of the Pope.

The procedure was employed in the past for figures such as Romuald, Norbert of Xanten, Bruno of Cologne, Peter Nolasco, Raymond Nonnatus, John of Matha, Felix of Valois, Queen Margaret of Scotland, King Stephen I of Hungary and Gregory VII. The practice remains valid even after the modern procedural reforms, being an instrument exclusive to the Roman Pontiff, generally reserved for "ancient" causes or for cults of already proven breadth.

itens.resumo: Official of the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints who, distinct from the postulator, provides technical guidance in the preparation of the "positio" and ensures the historical and scientific rigor of the dossier.
itens.corpo:
The relator is an official of the Dicastery (formerly Congregation) for the Causes of Saints whose function is to provide technical oversight of the investigation of a cause, guiding the postulator in the preparation of the «positio» — the volume that reconstructs the life of the Servant of God and demonstrates the heroic virtues, the martyrdom or the offering of life, as well as the reputation for holiness and the signs. The distinction of roles is central: the postulator represents the interest of the cause and acts as a kind of "advocate" for the candidate, while the relator is the expert of the Dicastery who ensures that the document gathers, rigorously and in accordance with the critical criteria of hagiography, the historical and testimonial evidence.

The office was reorganized by the Apostolic Constitution «Divinus Perfectionis Magister», promulgated by John Paul II on January 25, 1983, which reformed the entire canonization process. The document establishes that, for the study of causes, there exists in the Congregation a College of Relators, presided over by a Relator General. It falls to the individual relators to: study the causes entrusted to them, together with collaborators from outside the Congregation, and prepare the «positiones» on virtues or martyrdom; draw up in writing any clarifications of a historical nature requested by the consultors; and participate as experts in the meetings of the theologians, though without the right to vote. One of the relators is specially appointed for the «positiones» on miracles, taking part in the meetings of the physicians and in the congress of the theologians. After the examination of the diocesan phase in the ordinary meeting, it is the Dicastery itself that decides to which relator the cause will be entrusted.

The 1983 reform replaced the former system of direct confrontation between the promoter of the faith (the "devil's advocate," an office instituted by Sixtus V in 1587) and the postulator with a more collaborative work of historical and theological reconstruction, shifting the center of gravity of the process from the phase of debate to the phase of examination of documents. The Relator General, who presides over the session of the historical consultors, is assisted by assistants. Once the Dicastery has designated the relator, the postulator contacts him to prepare the «positio»; when it is completed, it is customary to deliver copies bound in red covers to the Relator General and to the relator who oversaw its preparation, as well as copies to the archive of the Dicastery. The requirement that the external collaborator reside in Rome during the preparation of the «positio» is recommended in the Guidelines for Postulators, in order to expedite the work. The «Studium», a body attached to the Dicastery created on June 2, 1984, was intended precisely for the formation of postulators and collaborators in the causes.

The practice has become an ordinary stage of the process. For recent causes, such as that of Dom Helder Câmara — whose process was opened on May 3, 2015, and whose Archdiocese of Olinda and Recife sent to Rome, in May 2021, about 20 boxes with 360 books of documents, totaling approximately 127,000 pages —, the Dicastery formally appointed, in July 2023, the Spanish Monsignor Melchor José Sánchez de Toca y Alameda as the relator in charge of overseeing the drafting of the «positio». Currently the Dicastery has a Relator General and several relators — professors and experts in theology, canon law and history — who succeed one another as causes are assigned to them, ensuring that each cause is investigated by a specialist before examination by the consultors. In the Dicastery's current structure, the Relator General is Rev. Angelo Romano.

itens.resumo: Meeting of the theologian consultors of the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints that examines and votes on the "positio" of a cause before the opinion of the cardinals and bishops.
itens.corpo:
Once it has been drawn up and printed, the «positio» of a canonization cause is submitted to a commission of theological consultors appointed by the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints — experts, often from outside the Roman Curia, who assess whether the evidence presented truly demonstrates the candidate's heroic practice of the virtues, martyrdom or offering of life. This technical examination, provided for by the Apostolic Constitution «Divinus Perfectionis Magister» of John Paul II (1983), is designated in the Dicastery's documents as the Special Congress of Theological Consultors. The «positio» is delivered to the theologian consultors together with the written votes of the historical consultors and any new clarifications from the relator; the task of these experts, together with the promoter of the faith, is to examine in depth the controversial questions before the cause moves on to the Special Congress.

The promoter of the faith (the "Prelate Theologian", formerly nicknamed the "devil's advocate") presides over the congress of theologians with the right to vote, prepares the report and takes part, as an expert and without a vote, in the meeting of the Cardinals and Bishops. A favorable vote of this congress is a condition for the cause to advance. According to the official note of the Holy See on the canonical procedure of the causes, if the majority of the theologians are in favor, the cause moves on to the examination of the Cardinals and Bishops, members of the Dicastery (the "ordinary congregation" or plenary). The votes and conclusions are gathered in a «Relatio et Vota», copies of which the postulator delivers to the secretary, to the promoter of the faith and to the archive of the Dicastery. When the congress points out difficulties, the postulator must present the appropriate considerations in writing, which are attached to the votes of the consultors; if the result is negative, the promoter of the faith informs the postulator about the procedure foreseen in the Ordinary Congress of the Dicastery.

When the cause involves the alleged miracle of a physical healing, a similar body — the Medical Board — examines the case beforehand from the scientific point of view, even before its theological evaluation. This medical examination has ancient roots: already in the Middle Ages medical experts were consulted, and on September 17, 1743 Benedict XIV created a specific roster of experts; later, on October 20, 1948, Pius XII established in the Congregation of Sacred Rites a Commission of Physicians and, on December 15 of the same year, a special Medical Council. John XXIII, on July 10, 1959, merged the two bodies into a single Medical Board, approving its Regulations. After the Constitution «Sacra Rituum Congregatio» (May 8, 1969), the Regulations were revised and approved by Paul VI on April 23, 1976. The current regulations of the Medical Board were approved on August 24, 2016 by Cardinal Pietro Parolin, by mandate of the Pope, and signed by the prefect, Cardinal Angelo Amato, and the secretary, Archbishop Marcello Bartolucci. The relator designated for the «positiones» on miracles takes part both in the meeting of the physicians and in the congress of the theologians.

Once the consultors have completed their stages, the dossier is presented to the Pope. If he authorizes the promulgation of the decree, the candidate receives the corresponding title — "venerable", if heroic virtues are recognized, or "blessed", in the case of martyrdom. The current structure of the Dicastery, with distinct colleges of consultors — one of historians and one of theologians —, goes back to the reorganization of the Congregation for the Causes of Saints: it was separated from the Congregation of Rites by the Constitution «Sacra Rituum Congregatio» of Paul VI (May 8, 1969), and received its current form and name through the Apostolic Constitution «Pastor Bonus» of John Paul II, of June 28, 1988. On June 5, 2022, with Francis' «Praedicate Evangelium», it came to be called the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints.

itens.titulo: "Nihil Obstat" for the Opening of a Cause
itens.resumo: Before accepting a petition to open a cause, the diocesan bishop must consult the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints and obtain its "nihil obstat" — the confirmation that Rome sees no impediment whatsoever. It is a negative declaration of impediments, not a positive approval of holiness.
itens.corpo:
The requirement to consult the Holy See before opening a cause of canonization entered the Church's legislation through the Instruction "Sanctorum Mater," approved by Benedict XVI on the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter, February 22, 2007, after being discussed by the Congregation for the Causes of Saints at its plenary session of April 24-26, 2006. The document devotes an entire title to the subject — Title VIII, "Nihil Obstat of the Holy See" — whose articles 45 and 46 provide that the diocesan or eparchial bishop, "before accepting the petition (libellus) of the postulator to begin the cause," is to ask the Congregation "whether the Holy See has any obstacle to the cause." The Instruction belongs to a line of norms that goes back to the Apostolic Constitution "Divinus perfectionis Magister" of John Paul II (January 25, 1983), which transferred the instruction of causes to diocesan bishops, iure proprio, and to the "Normae servandae in inquisitionibus ab Episcopis faciendis in Causis Sanctorum," approved by the same pontiff on February 7, 1983.

The request must be accompanied by a "brief account" with the biographical data of the Servant of God — date, place and diocese of birth and death, activity carried out in the Church — and a statement of the ecclesial importance of the cause (art. 45 § 2). The Congregation's reply reaches the bishop by letter, which becomes part of the acts of the process (art. 46). One detail that popular texts often oversimplify should be noted: the norm uses the formula "it is advised" (in the official English version, "would be well advised"), and not an absolute prohibition; article 40 § 1 itself makes acceptance of the petition conditional on prior verification that there exists an authentic and widespread reputation of holiness or martyrdom and of signs. The term "nihil obstat" ("nothing stands in the way") was not born in the causes of saints: its origin lies in ecclesiastical censorship of books, regulated by canons 822 to 832 of the 1983 Code of Canon Law, in which the diocesan censor (Censor Librorum) declares in writing that the work contains nothing contrary to faith or good morals before the Ordinary grants the "imprimatur." It is this technical sense — a negative declaration of impediments — that the formula retains in causes of canonization.

The consultation is not the only prior screening. Once the petition has been accepted, the bishop must also request the opinion of the Episcopal Conference (at least the regional one) — or, in the Eastern Churches, of the Synod of Bishops — on the advisability of beginning the cause (arts. 41 ff.). If a relevant obstacle arises from this exchange, the bishop informs the postulator so that he may possibly remove it; if the obstacle persists and the cause cannot proceed, the bishop communicates the decision by decree, stating the reasons (art. 44). Only then is the way open for the postulator to formally request the conduct of the diocesan inquiry.

The clause serves a twofold purpose. On the one hand, it standardizes practice among the hundreds of dioceses of the world and subjects each petition to a first examination on the merits by the central authority of the Church, reducing the risk that serious problems — historical, doctrinal, or a lack of reputation of holiness — would come to light only after years of local investigation. On the other hand, it prevents causes from arising out of passing emotion or devotional pressure lacking foundation. The very requirement of a reputation that is "spontaneous and not artificially produced," "stable, continuous, and widespread among trustworthy persons" (art. 7 § 2) is the substantive criterion behind the procedure. In recent practice, the "nihil obstat" has become a dated and public document in several cases — for example, the one granted for the opening of the cause of beatification of Father Cícero Romão Batista, dated June 24, 2022.

The institutional framework that now grants the "nihil obstat" has a long history. The body goes back to the Sacred Congregation of Rites, established by Sixtus V on January 22, 1588 with the bull "Immensa Aeterni Dei"; Paul VI, with the Constitution "Sacra Rituum Congregatio" (May 8, 1969), separated from it the Congregation for the Causes of Saints; John Paul II gave it its present form with "Pastor Bonus" (1988); and Francis, with the Constitution "Praedicate Evangelium" (March 19, 2022), renamed it the "Dicastery for the Causes of Saints," whose articles 98 to 102 define its competence. Beyond the causes of saints, the formula "nihil obstat" reappears in other canonical contexts, such as the processes for the dissolution of the marriage bond in favor of the faith, regulated by the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, in which the local authority must also obtain Rome's favorable opinion before forwarding the case. It is this precise sense — certifying that the Holy See sees no obstacle to the opening of the investigation, without canonizing or beatifying anyone — that gives the "nihil obstat" its technical value.

itens.titulo: The Dispensation from the Five-Year Waiting Period
itens.resumo: As a rule, five years are to pass after the candidate's death before the petition (libellus) opening the cause is presented; in exceptional cases, the Pope dispenses from this period and allows the cause to be opened almost immediately.
itens.corpo:
The common norm requires that five years pass after the candidate's death before the petition (libellus) that formally opens the cause is presented. The period was set by the «Normae Servandae in inquisitionibus ab episcopis faciendis in causis sanctorum», promulgated by the Congregation for the Causes of Saints by pontifical delegation and dated February 7, 1983, a few days after the Apostolic Constitution «Divinus Perfectionis Magister» of January 25, 1983. No. 9, a) of that document determines that, in recent causes, «the libellus must be presented no earlier than five years after the death of the Servant of God»; no. 9, b) adds that, if it is presented after thirty years, the bishop may proceed only after verifying, through careful investigation, that there was no fraud or malice on the part of the petitioners in delaying the start of the cause. The five years thus function as a minimum, and the thirty-year period as an upper limit of evidentiary convenience. The same requirement reappears in the Instruction «Sanctorum Mater» (art. 25, § 2), which forbids the postulator to present the libellus «before five years from the death of the Servant of God».

The waiting time is considered necessary so that the reputation of holiness may mature and be distinguished from a passing emotion, and so that the evidence — above all the testimony of eyewitnesses — may be gathered calmly. The Pope himself, however, may dispense from this period in extraordinary cases, when the reputation of holiness is already immediate and widely recognized. The dispensation is granted by the Holy See at the request of the diocese concerned, and the decision is usually recorded in a rescript of the Congregation (today the Dicastery) for the Causes of Saints.

Two recent and widely documented examples illustrate the exception. Mother Teresa of Calcutta, who died on September 5, 1997, had the dispensation communicated to the then Archbishop of Calcutta, Henry D'Souza, in a letter from the Congregation dated December 12, 1998, news that was made public in early 1999. The press of the time reported the grant as something rare and, in fact, it was the first time the five-year period had been waived since the modern process came into force. Sources differ as to the exact scope of the act: some describe a dispensation from the entire period, while the then prefect of the Congregation, Cardinal José Saraiva Martins, explained that for Mother Teresa John Paul II dispensed two of the five years. The cause was prepared quickly, and Teresa was beatified on October 19, 2003, before some 300,000 people in Saint Peter's Square, and canonized by Pope Francis on September 4, 2016, during the Jubilee for Workers and Volunteers of Mercy.

A few years later, John Paul II himself would receive similar treatment, and in his case the dispensation was complete. He died on April 2, 2005, the eve of Divine Mercy Sunday, which he had instituted, and the process was begun with unusual speed, amid the popular cry of «Santo subito!» heard in Saint Peter's Square during his funeral on April 8. On May 13, 2005 — forty-two days after his death, on the feast of Our Lady of Fatima and the 24th anniversary of the attack he had suffered in Saint Peter's Square —, Benedict XVI announced the dispensation from the five-year period while receiving the clergy of Rome in the Basilica of Saint John Lateran, reading the rescript in Latin and responding, it is said, «at the request» of Cardinal Camillo Ruini, vicar general of the Diocese of Rome. The cause was officially opened by Ruini on June 28, 2005. John Paul II was declared Venerable on December 19, 2009, beatified by Benedict XVI on May 1, 2011, and canonized by Francis on April 27, 2014, together with John XXIII.

The two cases show that the dispensation is rarely an isolated act of devotion: it usually comes accompanied by a strong popular outcry, by the explicit support of the diocese where the candidate died, and by circumstances regarded as exceptional by the Holy See. The mechanism, however, does not eliminate the remaining stages — it merely advances the start of the process, which still requires the examination of the virtues or of martyrdom and, for beatification, the verification of a miracle through the intercession of the Venerable; proof of this is that both Mother Teresa and John Paul II afterward went through, without shortcuts, all the ordinary phases up to canonization.
