itens.resumo: Every cause for canonization goes through two major stages: the investigation conducted in the diocese where the Servant of God died, and the subsequent examination by the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints in Rome.
itens.corpo:
The current structure of the two phases was established by the Apostolic Constitution "Divinus Perfectionis Magister" of John Paul II, dated January 25, 1983, which profoundly reformed the procedure and reorganized the former Congregation — previously part of the Congregation of Rites, separated from it in 1969 by decision of Paul VI —, providing it, among other things, with a College of Relators. With the Constitution "Pastor Bonus" (1988), the body came to be called the Congregation for the Causes of Saints and, with "Praedicate Evangelium" (2022) of Francis, it received the name Dicastery for the Causes of Saints.

The diocesan phase, or eparchial phase, is conducted by the bishop of the territory where the Servant of God died (art. 21 § 1 of "Sanctorum Mater"); when a presumed miracle is at issue, the bishop of the place where the alleged miracle is said to have occurred is competent (art. 21 § 2). The Holy See may, at the request of the bishop concerned, transfer competence to another diocese — for example, to the one where the most important evidence is found or where the Servant of God lived most of his or her life (art. 22), in which case written authorization from the competent bishop is required. It is up to the bishop to appoint a tribunal (with a delegate, a promoter of justice, and a notary), to gather testimonies from those who knew the candidate and all relevant documentation, and to submit the writings of the Servant of God to the examination of theologian censors, to verify whether they contain anything contrary to faith or morals. The acts are then sealed and sent to Rome.

In the Roman phase, the material received by the Dicastery is examined and, if it meets the requirements, receives a decree of validity. A relator appointed by the Dicastery itself then guides the postulator in preparing the "positio": the volume that summarizes the evidence gathered in the diocese and reconstructs the life of the Servant of God, demonstrating the heroic exercise of the theological virtues (faith, hope, and charity), of the cardinal virtues (prudence, justice, temperance, and fortitude), of humility, and of the evangelical counsels — or, in the case of a martyr, the martyrdom suffered out of hatred for the faith —, in addition to the reputation for holiness and signs.

The "positio" then goes to collegial examination. If the candidate lived a long time ago and there are no eyewitnesses, the study is carried out by the Dicastery's historical consultants; if there are direct witnesses, by the theologian consultants. The opinions may be positive, suspensive (when clarifications are requested), or negative (when the material needs to be restudied or redone). Once this stage is approved, the dossier goes to the Ordinary Session of the cardinals and bishops who are members of the Dicastery, who hold a new vote. With favorable opinions, it falls to the Pope to authorize the promulgation of the decree on the heroicity of the virtues — or martyrdom —, by which the Servant of God receives the title of Venerable. Only afterward come the following stages: the verification of a miracle for beatification and, in the case of the blessed, of a second miracle for canonization.

The two-phase system deliberately separates the investigation of proximity, carried out at the place of the events, from the doctrinal and historical judgment that belongs to Rome. This division lessens the risk of local pressures and ensures that the final decision (the Pope's formula defines canonization as an infallible and definitive act) rests on material verified in two distinct instances. The 1983 reform shortened the historically long durations of these processes, but the length still depends on the number of witnesses and experts heard in the diocese, the time needed to draft the "positiones", and the schedule of the consultants and the Plenary.

itens.titulo: Ancient Causes and the Historical Commission
itens.resumo: The Instruction «Sanctorum Mater» distinguishes "recent" causes — provable by eyewitnesses — from "ancient" ones, in which proof can come only from written sources; in every cause the bishop must appoint historical experts, who form the so-called Historical Commission.
itens.corpo:
The current legislation on the causes of saints distinguishes two types of process according to the type of proof available. According to the Instruction «Sanctorum Mater» (art. 29-30), a cause is "recent" when the heroic virtues, the martyrdom or the offering of life of the Servant of God can still be proved by the oral testimony of eyewitnesses — persons who knew him personally. It is "ancient" when such proofs can be drawn only from written sources, because no one is left alive who had direct contact with the candidate. In an ancient cause, the procedure concentrates above all on documentary investigation, although the bishop may still hear witnesses on the continued existence of the reputation of holiness or martyrdom and on the cult paid to the Servant of God in recent times.

This does not mean that the Historical Commission exists only in ancient causes: the same Instruction determines, in its art. 68, § 1, that "in all causes, both recent and ancient," the bishop is to appoint by decree at least three experts in historical and archival matters, who constitute the so-called Historical Commission. The difference lies in the relative weight of this work: in a recent cause, the evidentiary basis is the interrogation of witnesses; in an ancient cause, it is historical research that occupies the central place in the inquiry. For this reason the Instruction requires that the episcopal delegate himself, when the cause is ancient, be competent not only in theology and canon law, but also in historical matters (art. 54).

It falls to the experts to seek out and collect all the as yet unpublished writings of the Servant of God and all the historical documents, manuscript or printed, related to him; the search must be carried out in the archives of all the places where he lived and worked (art. 71). A simple list of the documents found is not enough: an authenticated copy of each is required, attached to the acts of the inquiry (art. 72). Once the research is concluded, the experts draw up a single, detailed report, signed "in solidum" by all of them, in which any differences of opinion among them may be recorded (art. 73-75). The office of expert cannot be entrusted to the postulator, the vice-postulator or their collaborators, precisely because the proofs must be gathered formally within the framework of a canonical process (art. 68, § 3).

This documentary model has ancient roots in the Church. The classic work of Prospero Lambertini — the future Benedict XIV, the "master" of the causes of saints —, «De Servorum Dei Beatificatione et de Beatorum Canonizatione», written even before his pontificate, systematized the subject and, among other cases, dealt with the causes of "confirmation of cult" (de confirmatione cultus). Here the Church distinguishes immemorial, or "ancient," cult from the ordinary process by virtues or martyrdom. The point of reference is the legislation of Urban VIII, whose decrees — issued between 1624 and 1634 and consolidated in the Apostolic Constitution «Caelestis Hierusalem Cives» of July 5, 1634 — reserved to the Holy See the right to beatify and canonize and forbade the public cult of anyone not beatified or canonized by it; they admitted, however, as an exception those who were already venerated "ab immemorabili tempore". For a cult to be recognized as ancient, it must go back at least one hundred years before that decree of 1634. Once immemorial cult is proved, the Congregation (today the Dicastery) may issue a decree of confirmation of cult, and the Servant of God is then recognized as Blessed — and, in the case of an "ancient Blessed," may be confirmed as such, after which the path to canonization may open (cf. «Sanctorum Mater», art. 33).

With the reform of John Paul II — the Apostolic Constitution «Divinus Perfectionis Magister» and the «Normae servandae», both of 1983 —, the historical-critical method was consolidated, which «Sanctorum Mater» of 2007 went on to detail. In the same reform, the Congregation was provided with a College of Relators, entrusted with preparing the «Positiones» («super Martyrio», «super Vita, Virtutibus et Fama Sanctitatis»), and the former Historical Section — created in 1930, under Pius XI — became the nucleus of this college, whose Ufficio del Relatore Generale preserves to this day the records of the historical causes.

In short, in an ancient cause the Historical Commission does not replace the testimonies as a mere formality: it assumes the central evidentiary function, critically reconstructing the candidate's life from archives and documents, under oath that it has neither altered nor destroyed any text and that it has gathered everything concerning the cause. The distinction between recent and ancient causes, the one-hundred-year criterion for immemorial cult and the requirement of suitable experts thus form the methodological axis by which the Church examines with historical rigor candidates who lived far back in time.

itens.titulo: The Postulator General of a Religious Order
itens.resumo: Religious orders and congregations maintain a "postulator general," appointed by the supreme moderator of the institute and ratified by the Dicastery, who represents the religious family before the Holy See in all of its causes of beatification and canonization.
itens.corpo:
Besides the postulator appointed for a single cause, there is the postulator general: a permanent office of institutes of consecrated life, societies of apostolic life and associations, responsible for simultaneously following all the causes of beatification and canonization of members of that religious family, conducted in various dioceses and countries. According to the Regulations for Postulators of the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints, the Postulator General is appointed — both for the diocesan phase and for the Roman phase — by a mandate issued by the Supreme Moderator of the Institute, with the consent of his Council; he represents the institute before the Dicastery and the local ecclesiastical authorities in all the causes of the institute itself and of the institutes aggregated to it, and this appointment must be ratified by the Dicastery. The role of postulators is framed by the pontifical legislation on the causes of saints, now found chiefly in the Code of Canon Law (and the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches), the Apostolic Constitution «Divinus perfectionis Magister» (1983), the «Normae servandae» (1983), the Apostolic Letter «Maiorem hac dilectionem» (2017), the Instruction «Sanctorum Mater» (2007) and the norms on the administration of the goods of causes. The Regulations themselves gather, in summary, all of this «peculiar pontifical law» for the use of postulators.

The Instruction «Sanctorum Mater» expressly provides (art. 15, § 3) that, if the postulator in the diocesan phase is the postulator general of an institute to which the Servant of God belonged, he retains his office also in the Roman phase, without need of a new mandate — a clause designed precisely for this stable office. Juridically, the postulator is responsible for representing the petitioner of the cause before the bishop, the Dicastery and the competent authorities, following all the stages of the canonical procedure; but his task is not reduced to this juridical aspect. The Regulations also assign him the mission of promoting and coordinating everything that serves to spread the candidate's reputation for holiness and to foster his intercession among the faithful, and he «assumes a particular responsibility, whether toward the Petitioner, or toward the Bishop and the People of God.» The Instruction further determines (art. 19) that the postulator must hand over to the experts all the documents of the cause that he possesses, but he may not himself juridically gather documentary evidence or testimonies — safeguarding the impartiality of the inquiry.

This spiritual and pastoral dimension was underscored by Benedict XVI when he received the College of Postulators on December 17, 2007, and by Francis, who on December 12, 2019 exhorted postulators not to be guided by material views or economic interests and not to seek their own personal affirmation.

A recent reform set unprecedented limits on this activity. The Regulations for Postulators, authorized by Francis on August 30 and signed by the prefect of the Dicastery, Cardinal Marcello Semeraro, came into force on October 11, 2021 — a date chosen in memory of the opening of the Second Vatican Council. It was the first normative document dedicated specifically to the figure and functions of the postulator. Two novelties stand out: cardinals, bishops, officials of the Dicastery itself, historical and theological consultors and medical experts may not be appointed postulators (art. 6a); and, except for the postulators general of religious institutes, no «ad casum» postulator may have, in the Roman phase, more than thirty active causes at the same time (art. 9). It is also required (art. 5a) that the postulator be a Catholic faithful of proven integrity and have adequate knowledge of theology, canon law, history and the practice of the Dicastery and, in the Roman phase (art. 5b), the diploma of the School of Advanced Formation in the Causes of Saints, maintaining a stable residence in Rome. The exclusion of postulators general from the limit of thirty causes is precisely the juridical recognition of the proper nature of this office: he represents an entire institute, not an isolated cause.

itens.resumo: The Church may bring together in a single ceremony martyrs from distinct persecutions, such as the 522 martyrs of the religious persecution in Spain beatified in Tarragona on October 13, 2013, the largest collective beatification in the history of the Spanish Church.
itens.corpo:
When a large number of the faithful are killed out of hatred for the faith in the same historical context of persecution, their causes may be conducted together and culminate in a single ceremony of collective beatification. The most significant example in recent times took place on October 13, 2013, in Tarragona, Spain: 522 martyrs of the twentieth century were beatified in a single celebration, brought together from 33 distinct causes of martyrdom from all over Spain. It is the largest collective beatification in the history of the Spanish Church.

The group included three bishops — Manuel Basulto Jiménez, Bishop of Jaén; Salvio Huix Miralpeix, Bishop of Lleida; and Manuel Borrás Ferré, auxiliary bishop of Tarragona —, as well as 88 diocesan priests, 15 priests of religious orders, 412 religious (among them numerous women religious, such as 27 Daughters of Charity of Saint Vincent de Paul and 68 Marists) and 7 lay people. Seven of the beatified were born outside Spain, although they died on Spanish soil, being natives of Colombia, Cuba, the Philippines, France and Portugal. The ceremony was presided over on behalf of Pope Francis by the then prefect of the Congregation for the Causes of Saints, Cardinal Angelo Amato; the Pope sent a video message for the occasion. Those present included about 104 bishops (eight of them cardinals), 1,386 to 1,400 priests, more than 2,700 to 2,800 religious and about 4,000 relatives of the martyrs, in a crowd estimated at more than 25,000 to 30,000 people gathered at the Tarragona Educational Complex; about 1.8 million people followed the live broadcast on two Spanish networks, and approximately 800 volunteers helped with the organization.

The choice of Tarragona as the venue was not by chance and had a twofold reason. The first is historical: in AD 259, in the city, Bishop Fructuosus and his two deacons, Augurius and Eulogius, were burned alive in the Roman amphitheater — the first martyrs of Spain. The second is that the largest contingent of the beatified — 147 in all — belonged to that ancient Spanish diocese, among them auxiliary bishop Manuel Borrás Ferré and the young seminarians Joan Montpeó Masip, aged 20, and Josep Gassol Montseny, aged 22. Most of the martyrs were killed during the Spanish Civil War (1936-1939), in the context of the religious persecution of the so-called Red Terror; two of them, however, had been killed earlier, on October 13, 1934. For this reason, the Spanish Episcopal Conference insisted that the new blesseds not be classified simply as "martyrs of the Civil War," but as martyrs of the Spanish religious persecution of the twentieth century — a distinction that seeks not to reduce martyrdom to a political-military episode. Cardinal Amato took up this point in the homily, stating that they were victims "of the persecution against the Catholic Church in Spain" and not of the civil war as such.

It should be noted that the promulgation of these grouped beatifications is part of a broader movement. Under John Paul II, 233 Spanish martyrs were beatified on March 11, 2001; under Benedict XVI, the 498 Spanish martyrs on October 28, 2007, celebrated in Saint Peter's Square (one of the largest collective beatifications in history, raising the total of beatified martyrs to 977); and, in 2013, the 522 of Tarragona, raising the total of Spanish blessed martyrs to 1,523, of whom 11 have already been canonized. It is estimated that the Spanish religious persecution of the twentieth century produced more than 10,000 martyrs, according to Church sources, and the beatification process had already been begun for about 2,000 people.

Despite the joint beatification, each martyr's reputation for martyrdom and the circumstances of his or her death were examined individually by the Vatican within the normal historical and canonical process; what is grouped is the final public celebration, not the rigor of the prior investigation of each case. A controversy marks the limits of this criterion: the Vatican did not include among the "martyrs of the Spanish Civil War" the roughly 16 priests (including Basques, such as the archpriest of Mondragón) executed by Franco's Nationalist side, among them clerics who tried to prevent killings — since they would not have been killed "out of hatred for the faith" (in odium fidei), a requirement for the recognition of martyrdom. The decision prompted criticism from relatives of victims and from Spanish political organizations, which considered it selective.

itens.titulo: Canonical Recognition and Translation of Relics
itens.resumo: During a cause, the candidate's mortal remains may undergo an official canonical recognition — which verifies their identity — and a translation to a new place of veneration, both subject to the prior authorization of the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints and to precise rules established in the 2017 instruction.
itens.corpo:
The Congregation for the Causes of Saints published, on December 8, 2017, the instruction "Relics in the Church: Authenticity and Conservation," which replaced the corresponding appendix of the instruction "Sanctorum Mater" (May 17, 2007). The document presents the complete canonical procedure for verifying the authenticity of relics and mortal remains, ensuring their conservation, and regulating their veneration, distinguishing four specific operations: canonical recognition, the collection of fragments and the making of relics, the translation of the urn, and the alienation of relics. It applies to diocesan bishops, to eparchies, and to those equivalent to them in law.

None of these operations may take place without the prior authorization of the Dicastery. It is up to the competent bishop to send the prefect of the Congregation the request for consent, indicating the exact place where the remains are kept (city, church, chapel, public or private cemetery) and, in the case of translation — that is, the permanent transfer to another place —, attaching the plan for the new placement. Before any operation on the remains, it is also necessary to obtain the authorizations required by the civil law of the place and the consent of the heirs. If the relics of a Blessed or Saint are to be taken on pilgrimage to other dioceses, the bishop needs the written consent of each prelate who will receive them.

The material procedure is detailed in the articles of the instruction. Once authorization has been granted, the bishop or episcopal delegate, the notary, and those in charge of the technical work go to the place where the relics are kept; once the urn has been removed, the notary reads aloud the authentic document of the last canonical recognition or of the previous pilgrimage, to verify whether what is written in it matches what is observed at present. If this document is missing, or if the urn or the seals are found broken, special caution is taken to confirm authenticity. If the recognition cannot be completed in a single session, the place is locked and the key remains in the custody of the bishop or the delegate. When the need for conservation treatments is evident, these are carried out with the most reputable techniques, according to the judgment of the anatomical experts. Once the body has been reassembled, everything is, if appropriate, placed in a new urn.

The instruction takes care to clarify a point that often causes confusion: the solemn translation of relics does not in itself constitute an external recognition of holiness — only miracles confirmed by the Church permit this official recognition. It is the decision of canonization, and not the solemnity of the translation, that inscribes the name in the list of saints. For this reason, the relics of the Blessed and Saints may never be exposed to the public veneration of the faithful without a special certificate from the competent ecclesiastical authority guaranteeing their authenticity.

The instruction itself classifies as "insignis relics" the body of the Blessed and of Saints, or notable parts of their bodies, or the entire quantity of ashes resulting from cremation. These insignis relics must be kept in special sealed urns, in places where security can be guaranteed, sacredness respected, and worship fostered. Competence over the authenticity and conservation of relics belongs to the Congregation for the Causes of Saints, while the regulation of the cult of sacred relics belongs to the Congregation for Divine Worship and the Discipline of the Sacraments.

itens.resumo: Distinct from the reputation for holiness during life, the "reputation for signs" is the opinion spread among the faithful that graces and favors have been obtained from God through the intercession of the Servant of God after his or her death — and it is one of the requirements that the bishop must verify before opening the cause.
itens.corpo:
The distinction between «fama sanctitatis» (reputation for holiness) and «fama signorum» (reputation for signs) is established in the instruction «Sanctorum Mater», published by the Congregation for the Causes of Saints on May 17, 2007, to regulate the conduct of diocesan inquiries. According to art. 5 § 1, the reputation for holiness is «the opinion spread among the faithful about the purity and integrity of life of the Servant of God and about the virtues he or she practiced to a heroic degree». Art. 6 then defines the reputation for signs as «the opinion spread among the faithful about the graces and favors received from God through the intercession of the Servant of God». There is also a third category, the reputation for martyrdom (art. 5 § 2), referring to death suffered for the faith or for a virtue connected with the faith. The whole Title II of the Instruction («Reputation for holiness or martyrdom and reputation for signs», arts. 4-8) is devoted to these notions.

While the reputation for holiness concerns the reputation for heroic virtue or martyrdom that the candidate had during life or at the moment of death, the reputation for signs refers to something later: the conviction that graces, healings and spiritual favors continue to be obtained through his or her intercession after death, a sign that he or she already enjoys the vision of God. The Latin text itself goes back to the doctrine of Benedict XIV, who in the work «De Servorum Dei beatificatione et Beatorum canonizatione» (book II, chap. 39, no. 7) described reputation as the esteem or common opinion born of devotion conceived in one or several places, so that the Servants of God are invoked by many in their needs. Prospero Lambertini himself, the future Benedict XIV, was the great eighteenth-century systematizer of this subject, and the text of the Instruction cites him in the footnotes to the definition.

This distinction has practical consequences in the preliminary phase of the cause. Before deciding to begin the process, the diocesan or eparchial bishop must verify whether, among a significant part of the People of God, the Servant of God enjoys an authentic and widespread reputation for holiness or martyrdom, together with an authentic reputation for signs (art. 7 § 1). The reputation must be «spontaneous and not artificially procured», and also stable, continuous and widespread among persons worthy of trust (art. 7 § 2) — a requirement that takes up almost literally the former canon 2050 § 2 of the 1917 Code, cited in the notes of the Instruction. It falls to the postulator to gather the documentation relating to both reputations and present it, on behalf of the petitioner, to the competent bishop, who evaluates it to ascertain the existence of the reputation and the ecclesial importance of the cause (art. 8). Only after an authentic and widespread reputation has been established may the bishop accept the petition (libellus) requesting the opening of the cause (art. 40 § 1).

In ancient causes, the investigation focuses above all on the work of historical and archival experts, but the need remains to question some witnesses about the current existence of the reputation for holiness and the reputation for signs (art. 30 § 2). Art. 34 provides, to this end, that the postulator present — in recent causes as well as ancient ones — a list of witnesses able to testify about the reputation still present among a significant portion of the People of God, «not forgetting those who could challenge such reputation»: the norm requires listing the opponents as well, so that the inquiry is not one-sided.

The reputation for signs also carries particular weight in two situations. In ancient causes, when the miracle formally proven by the ordinary process is lacking, an ancient and uncontested reputation for signs, together with immemorial cult, can ground recognition by the extraordinary path — equipollent canonization, in which the pope orders the cult of a saint long venerated without requiring the miracles of the ordinary process. Benedict XIV was the great theorist of this path; among recent cases are Hildegard of Bingen (May 10, 2012, 833 years after her death), Angela of Foligno (October 9, 2013), Peter Faber (December 17, 2013) and Joseph de Anchieta (April 3, 2014), as well as Marie of the Incarnation and Francis de Laval (2014), Joseph Vaz, Gregory of Narek and Junípero Serra (2015), Bartholomew of the Martyrs (2019), Margaret of Città di Castello (2021), the 21 Coptic Martyrs of Libya (2023) and Isaac of Nineveh, with Teresa of Saint Augustine and the Martyrs of Compiègne (2024).

itens.titulo: The Canonization of Carlo Acutis and Pier Giorgio Frassati (2025)
itens.resumo: On September 7, 2025, at the first canonization ceremony of his pontificate, Pope Leo XIV declared the Italian teenager Carlo Acutis and the university student Pier Giorgio Frassati saints, bringing together for the first time in a single rite two young blesseds whose canonizations had been postponed by the death of Pope Francis.
itens.corpo:
Carlo Acutis (May 3, 1991 – October 12, 2006) was an Italian teenager from Milan, passionate about computing and the Eucharist, who while still young cataloged dozens of Eucharistic miracles recognized by the Church on a website he programmed himself; he died of leukemia at the age of fifteen, in Monza, and became known as "God's influencer." He was beatified in Assisi in 2020, after the recognition of a miracle that took place in 2013 in Campo Grande, Brazil. Pier Giorgio Frassati (April 6, 1901 – July 4, 1925), a university student in Turin, a Dominican tertiary, an activist of charity among the poor and an enthusiastic mountaineer, died of poliomyelitis at the age of 24; he was known for the motto "verso l'alto" ("to the heights") and was beatified by John Paul II on May 20, 1990, who called him a "man of the Beatitudes."

The two canonizations were originally scheduled for separate dates within the 2025 Jubilee — Acutis on April 27, during the Jubilee of Teenagers, and Frassati on August 3, during the Jubilee of Youth — but were postponed after the death of Pope Francis on April 21, 2025. The newly elected Pope Leo XIV, who had begun his pontificate on May 8, 2025, presided on June 13, 2025, in the Apostolic Palace, over an ordinary public consistory in which he decreed that the two blesseds be inscribed in the register of the saints on the same day, September 7. At the same consistory he set October 19 for the canonization of seven other blesseds, among them José Gregorio Hernández and Bartolo Longo.

The miracle that opened the way to Acutis's canonization was the healing, in 2022, of the Costa Rican young woman Valeria Valverde, who had suffered a brain hemorrhage after falling from a bicycle in Florence; her mother made a pilgrimage to the blessed's tomb in Assisi, and the young woman recovered in a manner attributed to his intercession. The decree recognizing it was approved by Francis on May 23, 2024. For Frassati, the miracle recognized in a decree of November 25, 2024 was the healing of Juan Gutierrez, then a seminarian of the Archdiocese of Los Angeles, who had ruptured his Achilles tendon playing basketball in 2017; during a novena to Frassati he felt an intense warmth in his ankle and, on returning to the orthopedist, the doctor found that he had fully recovered. The healing was verified by the diocesan inquiry and by the medical board, the theologians, and the cardinals and bishops of the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints.

The ceremony was celebrated in Saint Peter's Square on September 7, 2025, making the two young men the first saints canonized in the pontificate of Leo XIV. According to EWTN, the Mass gathered about 70,000 people (Wikipedia records more than 80,000), and the pope concelebrated with approximately 2,000 priests. In the homily, Leo XIV departed from the practice of Francis, who usually said little about those being canonized, and spoke at length about the two new saints, emphasizing that cultivating holiness through "simple acts" — daily Mass, prayer, and Eucharistic adoration — is within the reach of every Catholic. Michele, Acutis's brother, read one of the readings. Acutis became the first "millennial" saint and is invoked as patron of the internet.

The speed of Acutis's process — canonized nineteen years after his death — generated controversy. In March 2025, a critical campaign gained space in the press, especially after a report in "The Economist" magazine, which interviewed childhood friends who remembered him as kind, but not necessarily pious; the Italian theologian Andrea Grillo became one of the main opponents. Among the objections raised are the family's wealthy background and the fact that his mother covered documentation and travel expenses of the cause, which critics suggested may have sped up the process. The postulator of the cause, Father Nicola Gori, stated that money did not influence the decision.

itens.resumo: An auxiliary figure to the postulator in causes of beatification and canonization, provided for in the Instruction Sanctorum Mater and in the Regulations for Postulators; he acts chiefly in the diocese or region where devotion to the candidate is alive, gathering and documenting graces and healings attributed to his or her intercession.
itens.corpo:
The vice-postulator is the figure who, in causes of beatification and canonization, assists or substitutes for the postulator in the diocese where the cause is being instructed. The distinction between the two arises from the very structure of the process: the postulator represents the petitioner of the cause before the competent ecclesiastical authorities, while the vice-postulator fulfills this representation at the local level. The Instruction Sanctorum Mater, published by the Congregation for the Causes of Saints on May 17, 2007 to regulate diocesan inquiries, establishes in article 14 that the diocesan or eparchial postulator may be substituted by others called vice-postulators, appointed by the postulator himself by means of a mandate drawn up according to law and with the prior consent of the petitioner of the cause.

The norm also defines their regime of residence and representation. Under article 15, during the diocesan inquiry both the postulator and the vice-postulator must reside in the diocese or eparchy in which the process is being instructed — a residence that, in the Roman phase of the cause, is transferred to Rome and is required of the postulator. Article 16 sets an important limit: in the Roman phase, the postulator may not be substituted by a vice-postulator in dealings with the Dicastery. The document appointing the vice-postulator is attached to the acts of the inquiry, and he is required to have the same preparation as the postulator — knowledge of theology, canon law, history and the practice of the Dicastery — as well as an oath to fulfill the office faithfully and to keep the secret of office.

The Regulations for Postulators, promulgated by Pope Francis and in force since October 11, 2021, specified these functions. The document provides that, in dioceses, the postulator may be substituted or assisted by one or more vice-postulators appointed with their own mandate and the written approval of the petitioner; it requires of them the same moral and professional qualities as the postulator; and it determines that the vice-postulator must always act according to the postulator's directives. It also clarifies that neither the postulator nor the vice-postulator is an employee of the Holy See, and therefore they may not benefit from the tax regime of article 17 of the Lateran Treaty.

In practice, it is the vice-postulator's task to gather accounts and documentation about graces and healings allegedly obtained through the intercession of the Servant of God, Blessed or Saint, forwarding the most substantiated cases for examination. The faithful who claim to have received favors normally turn to him, and it is through him that these episodes enter the process. In addition, there is the promotion of knowledge of the candidate's life and spirituality — through publications, electronic media, pilgrimages and celebrations — a task that sustains the reputation for holiness and signs, an indispensable condition for the progress of the cause over the years.

Concrete cases illustrate the role. In the cause of Father Eustáquio van Lieshout, the Dutch Fr. Alfredo Elfrink was appointed vice-postulator on February 5, 1956 and remained in the office until 1974, being credited with beginning the gathering of testimonies and documents that led to the official opening of the process. In the cause of Blessed Friar Bernardo de Vasconcelos, the vice-postulator Hugo César Peixoto Henriques received the decree of appointment from the hands of the Archbishop of Braga on October 27, 2022, and began to accompany the postulator who works in Rome. In Aracaju, the vice-postulator Friar Gleizer worked in 2024 during the phase of consultation with the bishops of Regional Northeast 3 and of Bahia, to publicize the opening of the cause of the Capuchin Friar Miguel.
